reason: Heart muscle fits around the hollow chambers and should enable them to squeeze.
expectation: The chambers will gain muscle that can squeeze them.

effect: The muscle lets the chambers squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so the pump still needs a way to direct flow.
reaction: The arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The valves should prevent backward flow during a squeeze.
expectation: The valves will direct blood forward through the chambers.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refill; the heart still needs a way to trigger repeated squeezes.
reaction: The paired squeeze and refill panels make the valves' roles clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells are shown generating a spreading electrical wave, which should coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The heart will gain a rhythm for repeated squeezes.

effect: The pacemaker completes the beating heart, leaving the blood and returning route to assemble.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and adjusting its rhythm was useful.
reason: Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites suggest it belongs inside the red-cell envelopes.
expectation: This will make red cells that can carry oxygen.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria; they still need to be added to the blood's fluid.
reaction: It was interesting that these cells make ATP without mitochondria.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to combine with the red blood cells.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The red cells and plasma form oxygen-carrying blood, ready to join the pump and vessel route.
reaction: The picture makes clear where hemoglobin and dissolved sugar are carried.
reason: Capillary networks should connect the arterial and venous vessels into a returning route.
expectation: The vessels and capillaries will form a connected circulation route.

effect: The capillaries connect the outward and returning vessels, and the circuit has named slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The empty slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart should fit the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted into the vessel circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart now occupies the pump slot; the circuit still needs its transport medium.
reaction: The heart's connection to outgoing and returning vessels is clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood should fill the circuit's transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will be fitted into the circuit, completing the pump and returning route.

effect: The blood completed the circuit, showing how the pump and vessels support exchange with tissues and return blood for another trip.
reaction: The exchange inset tied the completed construction back to the cells' need for supplies.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile: the squeeze and refill panels explained how they direct flow in both phases.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding blood to the named transport-medium slot was predictable once the circuit was assembled, though it completed the picture.

surprise.text: I was surprised that red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria or nucleus.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary; the item descriptions and named circuit slots made the purposes of the combinations clear.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested to see how the circulation connects with other systems, especially how it gets oxygen and nutrients for delivery to tissues.
